question: What does an embedding model produce from a piece of text?
options: A single relevance score between 0 and 1
A fixed-length vector of floats whose geometry encodes meaning
A list of the most important keywords
A compressed byte string of the original text
explanation: An embedding model maps any text to a fixed-length vector, a point in a high-dimensional space where relative positions encode semantic meaning learned from large corpora.

question: Two texts share no words but describe the same idea. Why can embeddings still rank them as similar?
options: Embeddings compare letters and spelling
The model maps meaning to vector direction, so same-meaning texts point the same way
They are compared by string length
It only works if they share at least one word
explanation: Embedding models are trained so that semantically related texts get vectors pointing in similar directions, regardless of shared words. Cosine similarity then scores that directional closeness high.
The vectors are perpendicular, so their dot product is 0 and cosine similarity is 0.0. Note the magnitude (the 5) is divided out; cosine ignores length and measures only direction.

question: You embedded your documents with model A. What must you use to embed incoming queries?
options: Any embedding model of the same dimension
The same model A
A larger model for better quality
A keyword tokenizer
explanation: Vectors are only comparable within the space of the model that produced them. Even matching dimensions from a different model live in a different space, so you must embed queries with the same model A.

question: A teammate says 'higher cosine similarity always means that passage answers the question, so just take the top score.' Why is this a misconception?
options: Cosine similarity can never exceed 0.5
Cosine measures topical/semantic closeness, not whether the passage actually contains the answer, so a related-but-unhelpful chunk can still score high
Cosine only works on numeric data, not text
Higher cosine actually means less similar
explanation: Cosine ranking is a signal of semantic closeness, not a guarantee of relevance. A closely related chunk that does not contain the answer can still score highly, which is why retrieval ranking is a signal rather than a proof.

question: How does choosing a higher embedding dimensionality (e.g. 1536 vs 384) trade off?
options: More dimensions are strictly better with no downside
More dimensions can capture finer meaning but cost more memory and slower search, with diminishing returns
Fewer dimensions always retrieve better
Dimensionality has no effect on index size
explanation: Higher-dimension embeddings usually retrieve a bit better but make the index larger and queries slower, so picking a dimension is a quality-versus-cost decision that directly sizes your vector store.
